description:
We are F4NTASTIC, a team of four enthusiastic students from Curtin University Malaysia, brought together by our shared passion for innovation, technology, and creative problem-solving. As participants in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are excited to challenge ourselves, explore new ideas, and push beyond the boundaries of what we thought was possible.

Our team is taking on the challenge of developing health monitoring software designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. With the unique physical and psychological challenges that come with space exploration, we aim to create an innovative, practical, and user-friendly solution that empowers astronauts to better understand, monitor, and manage their health and well-being.

We believe that great ideas come from collaboration, diverse perspectives, and the courage to think differently. By combining our individual strengths, creativity, and determination, we hope to transform our ideas into something meaningful that could contribute to the future of human space exploration.

For us, this challenge is more than just a competition. It is an opportunity to learn, grow, collaborate, and turn our curiosity into real-world solutions. We may be a team of four students, but we believe that with passion, teamwork, and a little bit of imagination, even the smallest ideas can lead to extraordinary possibilities.
summary:
ORBIT (Observational Risk Baselines, Investigation & Tracking) is an offline-first astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to transform health data into meaningful insights and actionable decisions.

During long-duration space missions, astronauts face physical and psychological risks while medical assistance may be millions of kilometres away. ORBIT addresses this challenge by enabling astronauts and health specialists to monitor health indicators, identify unusual changes, and coordinate follow-up actions.

Unlike conventional monitoring dashboards, ORBIT establishes personalized health baselines and investigates combined changes in heart rate, sleep, fatigue, stress, hydration, and blood oxygen. Its explainable alerts show the supporting evidence, helping users understand potential concerns rather than relying on unexplained risk scores.

Additional features include an interactive 3D body viewer, health trend visualization, daily assessments, Mission Replay, and an Action Centre for managing health-related follow-ups.

Designed for local operation without continuous internet access, ORBIT demonstrates how intelligent, transparent health monitoring could support astronaut wellbeing and informed decision-making, even millions of kilometres from Earth.
details:
ORBIT — Observational Risk Baselines, Investigation & Tracking

1. The Problem

As humanity ventures further into space, protecting astronaut health becomes increasingly challenging.

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to radiation, isolation, altered gravity, disrupted sleep, psychological stress, and other environmental hazards.

When astronauts are millions of kilometres from Earth, communication delays can make immediate medical guidance difficult.

Traditional health-monitoring systems often focus on displaying individual measurements. However, identifying meaningful changes, understanding their causes, and ensuring appropriate follow-up are equally important.

This is where ORBIT comes in.

2. Our Solution

ORBIT is an offline-first astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support both astronauts and health specialists.

Rather than simply displaying measurements, ORBIT connects health monitoring, personalized analysis, explainable alerts, and follow-up management in one integrated system.

The application allows users to record health measurements, monitor trends, identify unusual changes, and investigate potential health concerns.

ORBIT supports multiple health indicators, including heart rate, blood oxygen, blood pressure, sleep duration, fatigue, stress, hydration, mood, exercise, and other mission-related measurements.

3. Key Features

Personalized Health Baselines

Every astronaut has different physical characteristics and health patterns.

ORBIT establishes individual reference ranges using historical measurements instead of relying entirely on universal thresholds.

This enables the system to identify changes relative to each astronaut’s usual condition.

Health Drift Investigation

ORBIT investigates multiple health indicators together to identify patterns that may deserve attention.

For example, increasing fatigue and stress combined with declining sleep duration and hydration may be more informative than examining each measurement separately.

The investigation system provides explanations and supporting measurement comparisons so users can understand why a concern was flagged.

Interactive 3D Body Viewer

ORBIT includes a rotatable 3D human body visualization that helps users interact with relevant health indicators.

This makes the monitoring interface more intuitive and accessible.

Health Timeline

Interactive graphs allow users to examine historical health measurements, compare trends, and review data quality.

Mission Replay

Mission Replay enables users to revisit earlier mission timestamps and examine how health trends and investigation findings would have appeared at those moments.

This provides a way to understand how health patterns develop over time.

Action Centre

Identifying a concern is only the beginning.

ORBIT allows users to review alerts, acknowledge findings, assign follow-up actions, and document resolutions.

This creates a structured process for responding to potential health concerns.

Daily Check-in

Astronauts can record wellbeing information such as mood, fatigue, stress, sleep quality, and symptoms.

This combines physical measurements with important self-reported information.

Data and Simulation Lab

ORBIT includes reproducible simulated mission scenarios involving stable health conditions, gradual health changes, unusual measurements, poor-quality data, and recovery.

These simulations allow the system to be demonstrated and tested without requiring access to actual astronaut medical records.

4. Technology Used

ORBIT was developed using:

• React and TypeScript for the user interface.

• JavaScript and Node.js for backend functionality.

• Three.js for interactive 3D visualization.

• Recharts for health-data graphs.

• Vite for frontend development and building.

• Lucide for interface icons.

• CSV parsing tools for data import and export.

• Local JSON storage for persistent records.

ChatGPT was used as an AI-assisted development and documentation tool.

The application operates locally without requiring a continuous internet connection, an external AI API key, or physical health sensors for demonstration.

5. Creativity and Innovation

ORBIT’s innovation goes beyond displaying health measurements.

Its central concept is to transform passive monitoring into a connected process of observation, investigation, explanation, and action.

Personalized baselines help identify changes relative to individual health patterns.

Multi-signal investigations highlight combined deviations rather than focusing only on isolated values.

Explainable alerts provide transparent supporting evidence.

Mission Replay allows historical analysis without changing live records, while the Action Centre ensures that identified concerns can be followed through to documented outcomes.

Together, these capabilities demonstrate a more accountable approach to astronaut health monitoring.

6. Intended Impact

ORBIT aims to support astronauts and health specialists in understanding health changes and coordinating responses during long-duration missions.

Its offline-first architecture is particularly relevant to environments where continuous communication with Earth cannot be guaranteed.

Although ORBIT is a prototype using simulated and manually entered data, its design demonstrates how future health-monitoring systems could support greater astronaut independence and more informed medical oversight.

ORBIT is not a clinically validated diagnostic system. Operational use would require medical validation, approved mission procedures, and integration with appropriate monitoring equipment.

Our vision is simple:

Distance from Earth should not prevent astronauts from understanding and taking informed action on their health.
dataRefs: NASA — Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight
